questions.question: Describe the living and working conditions of indentured labourers on Natal's sugar estates.
questions.expected_answer: Housing: barracks of wood, iron or brick, crowded rooms, earth floors, few latrines and limited clean water. Health: dysentery, typhoid, hookworm, chest diseases; limited medical care; high death rates, especially among children. Work: dawn to dusk, nine to ten hours or more, six days a week; longer hours and night shifts in the crushing season from about May to December; planting, weeding and cutting cane in heat and humidity. Discipline: sirdars and overseers; wage deductions for missed days even through illness; some beatings though illegal; passes needed to leave; desertion was a criminal offence. Pay: 10 shillings a month rising to 14, with rations of rice, dhal, oil and salt. Conditions varied between estates, but the system favoured employers.

questions.question: Explain how indentured labourers resisted the system and how the government of India and commissions responded.
questions.expected_answer: Everyday resistance: working slowly, feigning illness, careless work, unauthorised absence. Desertion: leaving estates to seek better work. Complaints: walking as groups to magistrates and the Protector. Collective work refusals, a form of strike. Cultural resistance: building temples, celebrating festivals such as Deepavali and Muharram, keeping languages and music. Tragically, some took their own lives. Response: complaints reached India, which suspended emigration to Natal from 1866 to 1874; Natal passed new laws and appointed a full-time Protector; a commission investigated in 1872; the Wragg Commission of 1885 to 1887 took extensive evidence and recommended better medical care and supervision of employers, some of which was adopted.

questions.question: Who were the passenger Indians, and how did the Natal government and settlers respond to the growth of the Indian population?
questions.expected_answer: Passenger Indians arrived from the 1870s, paying their own fares; most were traders from Gujarat, Muslim and Hindu, some via Mauritius. They opened shops in Durban around Grey Street and across Natal, later the Transvaal and Cape. Free Indians who had finished indenture became market gardeners, fishermen and workers; by the 1890s Indians outnumbered whites in Natal. White traders and artisans saw competition. Natal passed the three-pound annual tax in 1895 on ex-indentured Indians who stayed, removed Indians from the voters' roll in 1896, and passed the Immigration Restriction Act and Dealers' Licences Act in 1897. Indians responded through the Natal Indian Congress, founded in 1894 with Gandhi, and the 1913 strikes and marches led to abolition of the tax in 1914.
